historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: GABA-B receptor agonists

starting.description: Before the reported 1962 synthesis, GABA had been observed to depress spinal-neuron excitability. Retrospective accounts describe the synthesis of a GABA derivative intended for central inhibition and improved brain access, and explicitly link later antispastic introduction to expected mimicry of endogenous GABA; a contemporary clinical paper discusses GABA's spinal inhibitory effects when introducing baclofen. These observations support an inferred development from GABA's known inhibitory biology; they do not identify the particular experiment or conference content that triggered Keberle's synthesis.

inspiration.description: Endogenous GABA and its observed inhibitory physiological effects; the specific experiment and conference content that informed Keberle remain unestablished.

steps.description: Curtis recalls that experiments beginning in 1958 found that applied GABA depressed spinal-neuron excitability, although its role as a spinal inhibitory transmitter was then uncertain.
Retrospective accounts describe synthesis of a GABA analogue intended to access the brain and exert inhibitory action; the inventor's exact initiating observation is not identified.
The 1969 inventor patent describes the chlorophenyl-substituted amino acid family and centrally inhibitory and muscle-relaxant activity; the history also recounts development toward antispastic use.

Clinical investigators discussed GABA's inhibitory effects on spinal neurons and reflexes when introducing baclofen; a 1971 placebo-controlled crossover trial reported greater improvement with the derivative.
Subsequent physiological testing associated baclofen with a bicuculline-insensitive GABA response, and the group named the receptor GABA-B in 1981.

design.description: Chemists synthesized a beta-para-chlorophenyl derivative of GABA with the aim of enabling central activity; the realized extent of brain penetration is separate from that aim.

circumstances.description: The described deliberate stage is the synthesis of GABA derivatives intended for central inhibitory activity, not a claim that all subsequent findings were planned.

limits: This record addresses baclofen, the sole assigned cohort member. The GABA-B receptor was distinguished after the analogue's synthesis and clinical development; later receptor-directed ligands are not separate founding branches for this cohort.
conflicts: S1 highlights similarity between Factor I and GABA in a 1959 experiment; S4 also reports important differences and rejects explaining all extract activity by GABA content. Similarity is not established identity. The issue does not establish which observations inspired Keberle.
gaps: The precise observation, experiment, or conference content that prompted Keberle's original 1962 program has not been identified from a direct inventor account. The 1972 inventor article on the chemistry and kinetics of Lioresal (S8) was located by bibliographic metadata but not read; the separate Keberle–Faigle 1972 chapter cited by Bowery was not read either.

The original 1980 Nature receptor experiment (S9) and 1959 Curtis–Phillis–Watkins spinal-neuron report (S10) were located but not read; their findings are attributed instead to the relevant discoverer retrospectives. S6 is abstract only and S1 was available only in the accessed historical passages.
